title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models
abstract: This paper demonstrates that large language models can memorize and leak individual training examples, including personally identifiable information. We propose a simple and efficient method for extracting verbatim sequences from a language model's training set using only black-box query access.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content:
Imagine you have a huge library with an infinite number of books. Each book represents a possible sentence or text. A language model is like a super-smart librarian who can predict the next word in a sentence. But, what if the librarian has memorized some of the books? That's what happens when a language model memorizes its training data.

We can think of this as a game of 'guess the book'. The librarian (language model) tries to guess the next word in a sentence, and if it's correct, it gets a point. But, if it's memorized the book (training data), it can just recall the answer instead of guessing.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
Our attack works by generating a large number of high-likelihood samples from the language model, and then sorting them using a separate reference model. We use six different metrics to estimate the likelihood of each sample, and rank the samples with an abnormally high likelihood ratio between the two models.

This process allows us to extract verbatim sequences from the language model's training set, including personally identifiable information.

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content:
We evaluated our attack on the GPT-2 model, and found that it can extract hundreds of verbatim text sequences from the model's training data. In the best attack configuration, 67% of candidate samples were verbatim training examples.

Our results show that larger models are more vulnerable to our attack, and that different attack configurations can change the types of extracted data.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Our attack has significant implications for the privacy and security of language models. It shows that even if a model is not overfitting, it can still memorize and leak sensitive information.

This has important consequences for the development of language models, and highlights the need for more robust privacy-preserving techniques.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content:
Our attack uses a simple and efficient method for extracting verbatim sequences from a language model's training set. It also highlights the importance of considering the memorization of training data in language models, and the need for more robust privacy-preserving techniques.

Our results show that larger models are more vulnerable to our attack, and that different attack configurations can change the types of extracted data.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content:
We provide a simple example of how to implement our attack using the GPT-2 model. This allows users to try out the attack for themselves and see the results.

Note that this is just a simple example, and the actual implementation may vary depending on the specific use case and requirements.
